content: Turkey coronaviruses are members of the Coronaviridae family and primarily infect turkeys, particularly young poults, causing gastrointestinal disease. These viruses are also referred to as Turkey Enteritis Virus, Bluecomb Disease Virus, or Turkey Coronaviral Enteritis. Transmission occurs horizontally through feces and can spread either directly or indirectly via contaminated objects (fomites). The disease has been reported in regions such as North America, Europe, and Brazil. A closely related disease in birds is avian infectious bronchitis. The clinical presentation of gastrointestinal disease in turkeys includes symptoms such as diarrhea, anorexia, and lethargy. Affected birds within a flock often exhibit darkened skin and ruffled feathers. In the United States, turkey coronavirus is one of the pathogens implicated in Poult Enteritis and Mortality Syndrome (PEMS), which affects birds up to one month of age. Mortality rates can be high in poults. Birds that recover from the infection develop lifelong immunity but may become carriers of the virus. Diagnostic methods for turkey coronavirus include necropsy, histological examination, indirect immunofluorescence, immunoperoxidase staining, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Treatment is primarily supportive and may involve the use of heat lamps, antibiotics, and milk replacers. Since the virus can persist within a flock, farms experiencing an outbreak should undergo depopulation to control the spread of the disease.
